_work.description: Selected plates from Geheime Figuren der Rosenkreuzer (Altona, 1785) — individual page scans uploaded to Wikimedia Commons. Cover/title page plus pages 13, 14, 16, 18, 28, and 50. The page numbers allow specific identification within the volume. Page 13 is confirmed as containing the Arbor Philosophica (alchemical tree). The Geheime Figuren is the defining emblematic text of the Gold und Rosenkreuzer order.
_work.blurb: Geheime Figuren der Rosenkreuzer (Secret Figures of the Rosicrucians, Altona 1785-88) is the central emblematic compendium of the Gold und Rosenkreuzer order — an 18th-century Rosicrucian brotherhood. Compiled by the order and attributed to Hinricus Madathanus Theosophus (Adrian von Mynsicht), it presents a systematic visual curriculum integrating Paracelsian alchemy, Kabbalistic mysticism, and Christian theology through elaborate symbolic diagrams encoding initiate doctrine on the three realms (Physica, Metaphysica, Hyperphysica). The most elaborately illustrated Rosicrucian text of the 18th century.
_work.rights: Public Domain. Published 1785-1788, well outside copyright.
_work.creator: Gold und Rosenkreuzer (attr. Adrian von Mynsicht / Hinricus Madathanus Theosophus)

entries.title: Geheime Figuren der Rosenkreuzer — title / frontispiece
entries.summary:
The title plate of Geheime Figuren der Rosenkreuzer (Altona, 1785), digitized from the Wikimedia Commons upload. This image presents the opening visual statement of the most important Rosicrucian emblematic compendium of the 18th century. Published in Altona (near Hamburg) by the Gold und Rosenkreuzer order, the Geheime Figuren der Rosenkreuzer ("Secret Figures of the Rosicrucians") claims to preserve Rosicrucian iconographic traditions from the 16th and 17th centuries, though scholars have established it as primarily an 18th-century production.

## Historical Context
The Gold und Rosenkreuzer was a Rosicrucian-inflected alchemical order that flourished in the Holy Roman Empire in the 1770s-1790s, claiming descent from the original 17th-century Rosicrucian brotherhoods. Their curriculum involved graded initiation, alchemical practice, and the study of illustrated symbolic texts — of which Geheime Figuren was the central teaching tool. Frederick William II of Prussia was reportedly a member.

## Authorship
The work is attributed to "Hinricus Madathanus Theosophus" — a pseudonym for Adrian von Mynsicht (1603-1638), a physician and alchemist. However, the 1785 edition was substantially compiled and augmented by the Gold und Rosenkreuzer order.

## For artists & game designers
The Geheime Figuren's visual program is one of the most elaborate and systematically developed in all Western esotericism — incorporating Kabbalistic, Paracelsian, Christian, and Rosicrucian symbolism into a unified visual curriculum. Public domain.

## Further reading
- Yates 1972 (definitive scholarly study of Rosicrucianism)
- McIntosh 1998 (Gold und Rosenkreuzer specifically)
- Wellcome Library: https://wellcomecollection.org/

entries.title: Arbor Philosophica / Alchemical Tree — Tree of the Philosophers (p.13)
entries.summary:
Page 13 of Geheime Figuren der Rosenkreuzer (Altona, 1785), uploaded to Wikimedia Commons. Tagged in Commons as "Alchemical trees," this plate depicts the Arbor Philosophica — the Tree of Philosophy — one of the central organizing images in the alchemical-Rosicrucian symbolic tradition.

## Iconography
The alchemical tree grows from the philosophical earth (prima materia) and bears fruits of alchemical knowledge. In the Llullian tradition that influenced alchemical illustration, the tree's branches represent stages of knowledge; adapted for alchemy, they represent stages of the Great Work or branches of alchemical theory. In the Rosicrucian tradition of the Geheime Figuren, the tree integrates Kabbalistic associations: the Sephirotic Tree of Life provides the structural template, with the ten Sephirot mapped onto alchemical stages, metals, planets, and spiritual virtues.

## The "Secret Tree"
The Latin tradition's "Arbor Philosophica" (also called "Arbor Secreta" or "Tree of the Philosophers") appears in the Pseudo-Lullian corpus, the Rosarium Philosophorum, and in Paracelsian literature. It becomes one of the emblematic cores of Rosicrucian illustration, representing the complete knowledge tree of initiated alchemical philosophy. Szulakowska traces this development from Lull through Paracelsus to the Rosicrucian compendiums.

## Attribution
The book is attributed to "Hinricus Madathanus Theosophus" (pseudonym of Adrian von Mynsicht), though the 1785 edition was substantially produced by the Gold und Rosenkreuzer order.

## For artists & game designers
The alchemical tree is the ancestral image for skill trees, tech trees, and research trees in games — here is its richest pre-modern iteration, laden with specific symbolic meanings for each branch and fruit. Public domain.

## Further reading
- Szulakowska 2000 (Rosicrucian alchemical trees)
- Principe 2013 (alchemy and philosophy)
- Yates 1972

entries.title: Human figure / Rosicrucian anthropology — p.14
entries.summary:
Page 14 of Geheime Figuren der Rosenkreuzer (Altona, 1785). Facing the alchemical tree on p.13, this plate presents a complementary element of the Rosicrucian symbolic system — likely either the cosmic man (microcosm/macrocosm figure) or a diagram showing the relationship between the human being and the alchemical principles. The facing-page structure (p.13 tree / p.14 human or companion diagram) is characteristic of the Geheime Figuren's pedagogical organization, which frequently pairs complementary images.

## Iconographic Context
The tradition of anatomical-alchemical diagrams showing the human body as a map of alchemical processes derives from medieval medical illustration, was developed through Paracelsian iatrochemistry, and reaches its most elaborate form in Rosicrucian works like Fludd's "Utriusque Cosmi Historia" and the Geheime Figuren itself. Szulakowska's research specifically addresses how the Geheime Figuren integrates anatomical and alchemical imagery.

## Further reading
- Szulakowska 2000, ch. 4-5
- Yates 1972, ch. 9-10 (Rosicrucian anthropology)

entries.title: Geometric Rosicrucian diagram — sacred geometry encoding cosmic structure
entries.summary:
Page 16 of Geheime Figuren der Rosenkreuzer (Altona, 1785). This plate presents one of the Geheime Figuren's systematic geometric diagrams, likely showing the relationships between the three realms (Physica, Metaphysica, Hyperphysica) or encoding the structure of a specific stage of the alchemical process in geometric form. The Gold und Rosenkreuzer curriculum made extensive use of geometric diagrams as mnemonic and meditative tools, encoding complex doctrinal relationships in visually clear spatial arrangements.

## Iconographic Context
Sacred geometry in 18th-century Rosicrucian alchemy inherits from the Renaissance tradition (Agrippa's "De Occulta Philosophia," Fludd's cosmic diagrams) and from the Masonic tradition of geometric symbolism (the Gold und Rosenkreuzer existed alongside and overlapped with Freemasonry in 18th-century Germany). The Geheime Figuren's geometric plates represent the systematic encoding of initiate knowledge in visual form.

## Further reading
- Yates 1972 (Rosicrucianism and Freemasonry)
- Faivre 1994 (esoteric tradition and sacred geometry)

entries.title: Alchemical process stages — the operations of the Great Work
entries.summary:
Page 18 of Geheime Figuren der Rosenkreuzer (Altona, 1785). This plate presents one of the core process diagrams of the Geheime Figuren — likely showing the operations of the Great Work (calcination, dissolution, separation, conjunction, fermentation, distillation, coagulation) in their sequence and relationships. The Geheime Figuren systematizes these stages in a visual curriculum designed for initiate instruction, with each stage having both a material-laboratory meaning and a spiritual-transformational meaning.

## Iconographic Context
The seven operations of alchemy are one of the foundational schemas in the alchemical tradition, traceable through Arabic alchemy (Jabir ibn Hayyan) into European sources and systematized in the 16th-17th centuries. The Geheime Figuren's version integrates these operations with the Rosicrucian three-realm framework and the Paracelsian Tria Prima.

## Further reading
- Principe 2013, ch. 2-3 (the operations of alchemy)
- Szulakowska 2000 (operations in Rosicrucian illustration)

entries.title: Rosicrucian mystery diagram — initiation and the hidden knowledge
entries.summary:
Page 28 of Geheime Figuren der Rosenkreuzer (Altona, 1785). Near the middle of Volume I, this plate presents one of the more elaborate mystery diagrams of the Geheime Figuren — diagrams that encode the secret knowledge of the Rosicrucian initiation in visual form. The Gold und Rosenkreuzer organized their teaching around a series of such diagrams, each of which was explained to initiates as they progressed through the degrees of the order. The diagrams combine symbolic imagery with inscriptions in German, Latin, and sometimes Hebrew, encoding multiple layers of meaning.

## Historical Context
The Gold und Rosenkreuzer of the 1770s-1790s operated as a secret society with elaborate initiation rituals, including the study and contemplation of symbolic images like those in the Geheime Figuren. Members included prominent Germans of the period, and the order had significant influence on early German Romanticism's interest in alchemy and occultism.

## Further reading
- McIntosh 1998 (Gold und Rosenkreuzer organization and rituals)
- Yates 1972 (Rosicrucianism and 18th-century esotericism)

entries.title: Final plate of Volume I — synthesis and completion
entries.summary:
Page 50 of Geheime Figuren der Rosenkreuzer (Altona, 1785) — one of the final plates of Volume I. At or near the end of the first volume, this plate presents a synthesis or culminating image of the systematic visual curriculum developed throughout the book. The Geheime Figuren's organizational logic moves from foundational cosmological diagrams through elemental and alchemical processes to spiritual and eschatological themes, with the later plates integrating what has been presented earlier.

## Structure of the Work
Volume I (Altona, 1785) contains approximately 50 pages of symbolic plates. Volume II (1786) continued the series with additional plates. A third section (1788) by J.D.A. Eckhardt provided supplementary material. The complete work became one of the most widely consulted Rosicrucian texts through the 19th century and into the 20th, influencing occultist groups from the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn to 20th-century neo-Rosicrucian movements.

## For artists & game designers
The concluding plates of systematic alchemical compendia often present the most ambitious and visually complex images — the synthesis of everything that came before. Public domain.

## Further reading
- McIntosh 1998
- Yates 1972
- Szulakowska 2006 (apocalyptic and Rosicrucian imagination)
